title: Dual-targeted CAR T-cell therapy shows promise in patients with treatment-resistant multiple myeloma
content:
A first‑in‑human study conducted by investigators at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute reported that the chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‑cell therapy TriPRIL reduced or eliminated signs of cancer in 12 of 15 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma.

TriPRIL, short for trimeric APRIL (a proliferation‑inducing ligand), targets two proteins on myeloma cells rather than a single protein, offering a dual‑targeted approach.

The study results were published in The Lancet.
summary: A first-in-human study by Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute investigators found that a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy called TriPRIL reduced or eliminated signs of cancer in 12 of 15 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. TriPRIL—short for trimeric APRIL (a proliferation-inducing ligand)—recognizes two proteins on myeloma cells instead of just one.

title: Self‑adjusting EEG helmet improves brainwave measurement reliability
content:
A new self‑adjusting electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring helmet has been developed to simplify and enhance brainwave measurements across a range of applications. The device is designed for clinical settings, rehabilitation, and brain‑computer interfaces (BCIs). It continuously monitors electrode‑scalp contact conditions and automatically readjusts electrode positions to keep contact stable.

By compensating for variations in users’ head shapes and hair conditions, the helmet reduces measurement variability. This improvement is expected to increase the reliability of EEG recordings, making the technology more practical for both research and clinical use.
summary: A self‑adjusting EEG monitoring helmet has been developed to enable easier and more reliable brainwave measurements in clinical settings, rehabilitation, and brain‑computer interfaces. It monitors electrode‑scalp contact in real time and automatically adjusts electrode positions, reducing variability caused by differences in head shape and hair, thereby improving measurement reliability.

title: Josie Peters reports squatting shortens bowel movement time
content: Josie Peters examines the claim that the average time required to pass a bowel movement is shorter when a person squats rather than sits, exploring the reasons behind this difference.

content: US secretary of state’s comments come as vulnerability in programming language Java highlighted There is “zero evidence” that a wave of IT outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access, affected Apple and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or are the work of malign actors, according to the US secretary of state. Marco Rubio said the US was “not under systemic attack” and a cascade of network problems was “not inter-related”.

title: Engineered nanosyringes provide new route into plant cells
content: Engineered nanosyringes offer a new method for delivering active proteins directly into plant cells, overcoming the significant barrier posed by protective cell walls and membranes. This approach aims to facilitate the study of intracellular processes, including cell growth and stress responses, which are controlled by proteins. By enabling the direct introduction of these molecular tools, researchers may gain new ways to engineer useful traits and improve plant characteristics.
summary: Engineered nanosyringes can deliver proteins directly into plant cells. The cell wall and membrane have made this delivery a major obstacle.

content:
Parents feel judged as their child moves from high school to adulthood.  

Parenting a teenager can be difficult, and many parents experience intense pressure to guide their child successfully through high‑school graduation and into the next stage of life.
summary: Parenting a teenager is difficult, and the pressure to guide a child through high school graduation to the next stage of life can be intense. This pressure is compounded by the feeling that parents are being judged during this transition.

title: Murdoch University and Taronga Zoo Release First X-ray Aging Guide for Echidnas
content:
Researchers from Murdoch University and veterinarians at Taronga Zoo have created the first detailed radiographic aging guide for short‑beaked echidnas.  

The guide offers a practical method for estimating the age of these iconic Australian mammals, covering the period from tiny puggles to early adulthood.
summary: Researchers from Murdoch University and veterinarians at Taronga Zoo produced the first detailed radiographic aging guide for short-beaked echidnas. The guide allows estimation of the age of these mammals from puggle stage to early adulthood.

title: Guide Moves Marine Protected Areas from Paper Parks to Real Protection
content: A new guide emphasizes that the success of marine protected areas (MPAs) hinges on effective planning, governance, monitoring, and enforcement, rather than solely on the amount of ocean designated for protection. This approach addresses the global goal of safeguarding 30% of the planet’s land and sea by 2030, moving beyond “paper parks” to ensure real protection.
summary: The study notes that protecting 30% of the planet’s land and sea by 2030 requires more than designating marine protected areas. Its success depends on how the areas are planned, governed, monitored, and enforced.
author: Phys.org

title: Miniaturization at amphibian origin reveals new ecological niche
content: Frogs, salamanders, and caecilians comprise over 9,000 living amphibian species, representing the smallest group of four-limbed vertebrates. Some species, such as Brachycephalus toads, measure less than 7 millimeters from snout to vent. This miniaturization stands in stark contrast to their ancient relatives, most temnospondyls, the extinct group from which modern amphibians arose. These ancestors were primarily aquatic or semiaquatic predators ranging from 1 to 5 meters in length.
summary: Modern amphibians, including frogs, salamanders, and caecilians, number over 9,000 species and are generally the smallest of all four‑limbed vertebrates, with some Brachycephalus toads measuring less than 7 millimeters. Their ancient relatives, temnospondyls, were aquatic or semiaquatic predators 1 to 5 meters long.

content: Writing is regarded as one of the most important inventions in human history. It has transformed how we share knowledge, communicate, and pass information from one generation to the next. The question remains whether writing has also altered the way we build sentences and the complexity of our languages.

The research highlights that while minerals are essential for bumblebee health, excessive amounts can be detrimental.
summary: Researchers published a study in Royal Society Open Science testing how buff‑tailed bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) respond to different levels of calcium, potassium, magnesium, and sodium in artificial nectar. title: Cannibal giant star caught devouring its companion in super-rare event
content:
Astronomers have observed, for the first time, a giant star expanding and engulfing its companion in a process known as the common envelope phase. This direct observation provides crucial insights into stellar evolution that researchers have sought for decades. In early 2025, a group of researchers noted that a star in the Andromeda galaxy had been gradually brightening since 2018. Later that year, the SPHEREx space telescope detected an extraordinary outburst from the same object, which was identified as a stellar binary. Over approximately one month, the object expanded at a rate of 330 kilometers per second and flashed with light 100 times brighter than its previous emission.

Viraj Karambelkar at Columbia University in New York and his colleagues followed up on the object, designated AT 2025abao, using the James Webb Space Telescope. By analyzing all available data, they determined that AT 2025abao was undergoing a process where a red giant star expands and engulfs its smaller companion. The smaller star spirals toward the core of the larger star and is eventually torn apart. Karambelkar stated that the team was able to observe all different phases of this process, including the quiescent system, the moment the stars touched, the inspiral, and the major outburst in 2025.

The outburst originated from the moment the smaller star, nicknamed Small Bao, was ripped apart at the core of the larger star, Big Bao. Jason Nordhaus at the Rochester Institute of Technology, who was not involved in the research, described this as the most uncertain and critical phase in a star's evolution. He noted that nearly one-third of stars will go through this phase at some point in their lifetimes, with a higher percentage if considering objects that engulf non-stellar bodies like planets. Because the phase lasts only a few years of a star’s billions-of-years lifespan, it is a rare and challenging event to observe.

The research revealed that the common envelope phase lasted longer than previously expected, radiating energy carried to the surface of the expanded red giant by convection. Nordhaus explained that the physics involved differs significantly from prior assumptions, which held that convection would not be important and that energy from the smaller star would immediately puff up the larger star's atmosphere. Karambelkar emphasized that catching the event in the act allowed the team to trace exactly how the process occurs, providing a new method to probe the interiors of giant stars.

Looking ahead, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope are beginning to observe large portions of the sky. These instruments should enable astronomers to detect many more of these events in the coming years, further enhancing understanding of these stellar interactions. The findings are published in Nature with the DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11221-z.
summary: Artist’s impression of a large star absorbing the matter of another Nazarii_Neshcherenskyi/Shutterstock For the first time, astronomers have seen a star expand and gobble up its stellar companion. Watching this process as it happened has given researchers crucial insights into the evolution of stars that they have been seeking for decades.
author: New Scientist

title: NIST researchers demonstrate quantum position verification protocol
content: NIST’s campus in Boulder, Colorado NIST Financial institutions and critical infrastructure could be made far more secure in the near-future using quantum particles. For years, researchers have predicted that quantum particles could enable someone to share their location, and to verify someone else’s, in a way that is exceedingly difficult to hack. This would allow one branch of a bank to confirm that a request for funds or client information is coming from another branch and not from a hacker. Likewise, hackers could be stopped from trying to remotely control a power grid, a nuclear plant – or even commercial freezers, which have recently been hacked across Europe. Gautam Kavuri at the University of Colorado Boulder and his colleagues have now shown that quantum devices really can provide such location verification, offering a level of security impenetrable to most hackers. Advertisement Inside the company selling quantum entanglement “From a security perspective, it’s sort of the gold-plated Rolls Royce of protocols. It’s got the best security you can have in principle, while making the least assumptions,” says team member Krister Shalm at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Colorado. “And you can actually do it.” In the researchers’ experiment, two verifier devices had to confirm the location of a third device called the prover. Each device was in a different location: the verifiers were 195 metres apart in different labs and the prover was in a third location between them. Kavuri says it was important for these devices to be in different rooms on the NIST campus, rather than all in the same lab, because this is closer to a practical scenario in the real world. The devices were connected with electrical cables and optical fibres and could exchange quantum particles of light that had been connected into pairs through the inextricable link of quantum entanglement. To begin the new quantum position verification (QPV) protocol, a verifier would send one photon from an entangled pair to the prover and, simultaneously, each verifier would also send a random number that instructed the prover on which particle property to measure. Next, the prover sent the outcome of that measurement to both verifiers. They used the time it took to receive this information to calculate the prover’s position. Free newsletter Sign up to The Weekly Sign up to newsletter Several quantum tricks made this procedure more secure than any conventional one. First, quantum information, such as that carried by particles of light, can never be copied or cloned surreptitiously. Additionally, the researchers leveraged a procedure called a Bell test, which is specific to entangled particles, and would be failed if a hacker tampered with them. The net effect was that any conventional strategy for faking the position would set off one of these quantum safeguards. In this way, the new work builds on past theoretical results that promise to make it nearly impossible for position verification to be hacked once you go beyond conventional communication and turn to quantum tricks, says Philip Verduyn Lunel at Sorbonne University in Paris. “QPV is a possible ‘killer app’ for quantum networks,” says Wolfgang Löffler at Leiden University in the Netherlands. Although several outstanding problems will need to be solved to make this protocol fully practical, the new experiment is a big step towards doing just that, he says. Löffler says that it must have been a massive effort to get all the timings and device fidelities just right. City-wide quantum communication network in China is most advanced yet A network that connects quantum devices and a central server that spans Hefei, China, can allow multiple secure quantum chats at once “They have really pushed all the experimental constraints to their limit,” says Verduyn Lunel. Robert Malaney at the University of New South Wales Sydney says the new protocol is attractive for practical applications in part because it is compatible with conventional wireless communication infrastructure. But if several nefarious actors could quantum entangle devices that they use for hacking, they could still cheat the current implementation of the protocol, he says. This is because, in this case, the hackers could perform some computations without having to send each other extra messages. Going forward, the protocol must also be adapted to work over longer distances, which could require new computational steps and devices, says Florian Speelman at the University of Amsterdam. This will be a challenge, but the new work still moves us closer to QPV being a reality, he says. The researchers are now working on tweaking their protocol to make it more resilient to any photons getting lost as well as being more impervious to hackers looking to leverage quantum entanglement, says team member Yanbao Zhang at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee. Journal Reference: Nature DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3
summary: Researchers at NIST in Boulder used entangled photons to verify a device's location between two verifiers 195 metres apart. The protocol, which relies on quantum entanglement and Bell tests, could secure financial institutions and critical infrastructure against hacking.
author: New Scientist

title: Homo erectus lived on mainland Asia 215,000 years longer than previously believed
content:
New research has pushed back the last known appearance of Homo erectus on mainland Asia by more than two hundred thousand years.  Teeth recovered from two limestone caves in southern China – Baxian and Naxian – have been securely dated to as recent as 184,000 years ago, a date that extends the species’ presence on the continent by 215,000 years beyond the previously accepted limit of about 400,000 years ago.

The two caves, located roughly 15 kilometres apart, yielded over 18,000 mammal fossils, including nine hominin teeth.  Morphological analysis and CT scans identified eight of those teeth as belonging to Homo erectus; the ninth could not be assigned based on shape alone.  To confirm the identity of the hominin remains, the team extracted proteins from the dentine of five teeth, including the ambiguous ninth tooth.  The protein ameloblastin contained a signature that had been seen only in other Asian Homo erectus fossils and not in any other ancient hominin, strengthening the case that the teeth were indeed from Homo erectus individuals.

The researchers dated the teeth themselves, the surrounding sediments, and mineral formations in the caves.  The combined data placed the teeth between 324,000 and 184,000 years old, with the dates from different layers and formations correlating well.  The isotopic analysis of the teeth indicated that the Homo erectus population lived in a tropical rainforest environment, with animal bones from rainforest species such as rhinoceros and elephant.  Strontium isotope levels suggested that the individuals had moved considerable distances within the rainforest during early life.

The discovery not only extends the known temporal range of Homo erectus on mainland Asia but also suggests the existence of a genetically distinct population, separated from other known groups by geographic distance.  It raises the possibility that these late‑surviving Homo erectus could have encountered later hominin groups such as the Denisovans, which emerged in East Asia around the same period.
summary: Preserved teeth from two caves in southern China were dated to 184,000 years ago, showing Homo erectus survived on mainland Asia until then, 215,000 years longer than previously believed. Protein analysis of the teeth confirmed their identity as Homo erectus.

content:

The breakthrough could pave the way for less invasive treatments using injectable particles and wearable magnetic headbands.

content: A recent breakthrough in superconductivity research shows that one of the key ingredients—electron pairing—can occur at room temperature. Scientists found that electrons can form stable pairs at temperatures far higher than previously thought, indicating that another, as yet unidentified, obstacle may be preventing the realization of room‑temperature superconductors.

title: Maritime (YC F26) launches managed cloud for production AI agents
content:
Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime, a Y Combinator F26 startup, have launched an agent-native cloud platform designed to manage production AI agents. The company provides a managed cloud environment that handles custom environments and lifecycle management, offering each agent an isolated, persistent microVM with a configurable environment. Maritime aims to address infrastructure challenges that extend beyond basic sandboxing, providing composable services such as provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, scheduling, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, and per-agent spend tracking.

The founders argue that while many sandbox companies in San Francisco offer solutions, these typically address only a small portion of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. They describe the common approach as purchasing bare metal servers from providers like Hetzner or OVH Cloud, using Firecracker to slice servers into virtual machines, and selling those VMs with low margins. Maritime’s team spoke with hundreds of companies building AI agents, including developers of personal assistants, coding agents, and specialized healthcare agents. They identified that even after selecting a sandbox provider, companies must build additional infrastructure to get their agents working, creating significant friction.

Three primary points of friction were identified: agent lifecycle management, custom environments, and cost optimization. Lifecycle management requires building features such as sleep/wake capabilities, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing, spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. Custom environments are necessary because production agents have varying needs, such as Windows applications, Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software, specific dependencies, access to private networks, residential IPs, or restricted network access.

Cost optimization is another critical challenge. For example, a personal assistant sold for $20 per month would incur roughly $29 per month in sandbox costs if a $0.04/hour sandbox runs continuously, excluding LLM inference and storage. Maritime addresses this by optimizing sandbox usage through auto-snapshotting, event-driven operations, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, and cold-tiering snapshots. The platform incorporates scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, and hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering to balance cost with performance metrics like latency.

As a result of these optimizations, Maritime states that its service costs $1 per month for a 2GB RAM agent with unlimited usage, with additional resources available as needed. The founders, who started Maritime in March, previously conducted research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure and agent coordination protocols. Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT, while Ary conducted research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. They launched the company after facing issues deploying agents to the cloud during their research. The team is currently seeking feedback from other developers regarding the workarounds they have had to build on top of sandboxes and whether Maritime’s features align with their needs.
summary: Maritime offers an agent-native cloud that provides isolated microVMs and lifecycle management services to address infrastructure gaps left by sandbox providers. The platform optimizes costs through features like scale-to-zero and snapshot tiering, allowing users to run a 2GB RAM agent for $1 per month.
author: Hacker News

title: Osmo AI Startup Claims Human‑Level Smell Model; Southwest Hydropower Drops
content:
The Download, a weekday newsletter that delivers a daily snapshot of technology news, opens this edition with two stories that illustrate the breadth of current innovation and its limits. The first story focuses on a New Jersey‑based startup called Osmo, which claims its artificial‑intelligence system can detect odors with a sensitivity comparable to that of a human nose. The second story reports a sharp decline in hydropower output across the U.S. Southwest, a trend linked to an extended drought and the broader impacts of climate change.

Osmo’s laboratory team is attempting to catalog every odor on Earth. Researchers record descriptors such as “nutty,” “peachy,” and “marine” and cross‑reference those notes with detailed chemical analyses. The data set is used to train what the company calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. According to founder Alex Wiltschko, the model has already reached “human‑level olfactory intelligence” and is being employed by fragrance brands to design new scents.

Wiltschko also outlines broader ambitions for the technology. Osmo envisions applications that extend beyond perfumery, including the detection of counterfeit goods and the diagnosis of diseases. While the company highlights these potential uses, it has not yet demonstrated the technology’s effectiveness in these areas.

The hydropower story comes from new data released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Between April and August, the Southwest generated 28 % less electricity from hydropower than the 10‑year average. Most U.S. hydropower plants rely on dams that create reservoirs, but an extreme, prolonged drought has lowered water levels in the region’s two largest reservoirs to dangerously low levels. Climate change is cited as an additional factor that is intensifying the pressure on these water resources.

Together, the two stories underscore the dual nature of technological progress. On one hand, Osmo’s AI nose represents a leap forward in sensory computing, while on the other, the Southwest’s hydropower struggles highlight the vulnerability of renewable energy sources to environmental change. The Download’s coverage reminds readers that advances in one domain can coexist with challenges in another, shaping the complex landscape of modern technology.
summary: Osmo, an AI startup, says its smell model has reached human‑level olfactory intelligence and is helping fragrance brands design scents. US Southwest hydropower generation fell 28% from April to August due to drought, leaving reservoirs at dangerously low levels.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: The Verge explains how it selects Black Friday deals
content:
The Verge has been inundated with Black Friday offers for the past month, with dozens of press releases arriving each day from brands large and small that hope the publication will publicize their deals. The Verge notes that most companies do not provide the context the site needs to vet offers, and that many indicators of a good deal are confusing for both reporters and shoppers.

Groundwork Collaborative’s recent study of Amazon’s deal presentation illustrates this confusion. The researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, finding that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon did not actually offer savings during the sales events. They also reported that almost a tenth of the deals examined were more expensive during the sales than on some days in the month leading up to them. In a statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow, an Amazon spokesperson explained that the “List Price” can be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork’s research had suggested, and that it is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers.

The Verge’s approach to covering deals is therefore careful and selective. Deals must meet the site’s standards, which include a genuine price drop and a discount that is worth attention. The publication also considers factors such as the product’s quality, the duration of the offer, membership requirements, and whether the retailer is familiar to the team. Recent price hikes caused by RAMageddon and higher tariffs have sometimes meant that a “deal” price is close to the original sticker price, yet the Verge still evaluates whether the offer is worthwhile.

To stay informed about price changes, the Verge uses free tracking tools such as CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, and Amazon’s Alexa for Shopping, which provide historical pricing data. While the tools are helpful, none are perfect, and the Verge acknowledges that they sometimes do not display the record‑low prices it has covered. Ultimately, the publication casts a wide net across categories but publishes only a handful of standouts—headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart‑home tech, and the like—that meet its criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.
summary: The Verge vets Black Friday deals by verifying price drops, product quality, and discount authenticity using tools such as CamelCamelCamel, Keepa, and Amazon’s historical pricing data. It also avoids deals that are inflated, short‑lived, or only available through obscure retailers, following findings that many Amazon “deals” are misleading.
author: The Verge

title: Mobility startup spun from Rivian pauses e‑bike deliveries over software bugs
content:
A mobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year has announced a pause in customer deliveries of its first e‑bikes. The company said in an email sent this week that the wait for buyers has lengthened further.

The startup has already faced supply‑chain headaches and the challenge of building a futuristic bike that relies almost entirely on software. Those hurdles have slowed the rollout of its Launch Edition TM‑B models.

The company identified “a few software‑based issues, such as charging behavior,” affecting some of the Launch Edition TM‑B bikes. Consequently, it is suspending customer deliveries until the problems can be resolved.
summary: The mobility startup spun out of Rivian last year is pausing deliveries of its Launch Edition TM‑B e‑bikes. The pause follows the identification of software‑based issues, such as charging behavior, that affect some bikes.
author: The Verge

title: Meta’s Instagram school safety program aimed to boost teen user acquisition
content:
Meta’s initiative to make Instagram safer for schools was driven by user‑acquisition goals. According to NPR, internal documents show Meta sought to increase acquisition, friending, and invites.  

Documents from a group of child‑safety lawsuits mention Project Gryffindor, a school program designed to fuel organic and unattributed acquisition of users. An internal presentation from November 2023 stated the program would give teens a new reason to join or find more value in Instagram. The documents indicate Meta considered goals beyond teen safety when launching the School Partnership Program.
summary: Meta’s Instagram school safety program aimed to boost teen user acquisition.
author: The Verge

title: The Verge releases 2026 holiday gift guide for travelers
content: Everyone has that traveler in their life. That person who feels more at home on a 14-hour train ride than a quiet Sunday on the couch. They speak multiple languages, have a gut like a goat, and make friends wherever they go. Whether they're your kindred spirit or the person you live vicariously through, one thing never changes: They always need new gear. That's what makes travelers so fun to buy for. But you don't want to get them just anything. The key is to find that clever gift even they didn't know they needed, and that's where we come in. From streaming gadgets for the hotel to portable espresso makers and high-capacity charger …
summary: The Verge has published a 2026 holiday gift guide for travelers. It highlights gifts such as streaming gadgets for hotels, portable espresso makers and high‑capacity chargers.
author: The Verge

title: Nvidia ships Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it fastest product ramp amid AI pause debate
content:
Nvidia has begun shipping its most advanced AI‑computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, and has described the rollout as the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” The announcement comes amid a period of heightened scrutiny over the capabilities of large AI models.

This summer, OpenAI halted its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face. Early evidence suggested that the next model could independently discover and exploit security flaws, prompting the pause. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged a slowdown in the development of the most powerful AI models, warning that they could be used to launch cyberattacks or become difficult for their creators to control.

The contrast between rapid hardware deployment and cautious model development has left investors questioning how demand for AI chips will evolve during this uncertain phase of the AI boom.
summary: Nvidia ships Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it fastest product ramp amid AI pause debate.
author: The Verge

title: 8BitDo GC Bluetooth Gamepad preorder opens at $49.99, ships Dec 10
content:
8BitDo’s new GC Bluetooth Gamepad is positioned as a modern update to the Nintendo GameCube’s WaveBird controller.  The design closely follows the GameCube’s original layout, preserving its unique button arrangement, thumbstick shape, and shoulder buttons.  In contrast, 8BitDo’s earlier 64 model was a loose remake of the Nintendo 64’s triple‑grip controller, which omitted the centered analog stick.

The GC Bluetooth Gamepad is now available for preorder at $49.99 in orange or purple, with shipping slated to begin on December 10th.  The price is lower than Nintendo’s $69.99 wireless remake of the GameCube controller.
summary: 8BitDo GC Bluetooth Gamepad preorder opens at $49.99, ships Dec 10.
author: The Verge

title: Shelly launches Neo Smart Water Valve that auto‑shuts water on leak detection
content:
Shelly has introduced the Neo Smart Water Valve, a device that can be installed on a home’s main water line and automatically shut off flow when one of the company’s leak sensors detects a problem. The valve complements Shelly’s previously released leak sensor, which retails for $28 and runs on a battery for two years.

The Neo Smart Water Valve is sold through Shelly’s online store for $499.99, with additional costs for professional installation if the buyer does not feel comfortable installing it themselves. The valve is built for a standard U.S. 1‑inch thread connection.
summary: Shelly announced the Neo Smart Water Valve, which can be installed on a home’s main water line and automatically shuts off flow when a Shelly leak sensor detects a problem. The valve sells for $499.99 through Shelly’s online store, with additional installation costs if the buyer does not install it themselves.
author: The Verge

title: Disney unveils AI‑powered Star Wars animatronics that interact with guests
content:
Disney parks’ animatronic characters have traditionally followed set routines or relied on hidden puppeteers to create the illusion of spontaneity. Walt Disney Imagineering R&D says this may soon change.  

The company has unveiled three new Audio‑Animatronic prototypes—Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a, and Jibu Bre’a—that use Amazon’s AWS cloud and AI to react to guests in real time. These figures are based on the Anzellans, alien characters that appeared in The Mandalorian and the Grogu film.  

If successful, the prototypes could allow future Disney attractions to feature animatronics that respond uniquely to each visitor’s interactions.
summary: Walt Disney Imagineering R&D revealed three new Audio‑Animatronic prototypes that use Amazon’s AWS cloud and AI to respond to guest interactions in real time. The animatronics, named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre'a, and Jibu Bre'a, are based on the Anzellans alien characters featured in The Mandalorian and the Grogu film.
author: The Verge

title: Ars Technica review of Grand Theft Auto VI highlights crime action and domestic life contrast
content: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers. Read full article Comments
summary: The review notes Grand Theft Auto VI juxtaposes high‑octane criminal scenes with mundane tasks like building an Ikea‑style coffee table. It describes a reimagined Vice City that is detailed and technically impressive, created with a reported billion‑dollar budget over roughly a decade by thousands of Rockstar staff.
author: Ars Technica

title: Voyager 1 reaches one light‑day distance as historian uncovers Golden Record details
content:
Voyager 1, humanity’s most distant spacecraft, has now traveled a distance of one light‑day from Earth. Launched in 1977, the probe was originally tasked with fly‑by missions to Jupiter, Saturn and Saturn’s moon Titan, and it entered interstellar space in 2012.

The spacecraft carries a “commemorative phonograph record,” commonly known as the Golden Record, intended as a message to any future discoverer and as a nod to the centennial of the recording medium. While researching the record’s history, historian Glen Swanson identified a previously overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicate copies that were produced and distributed nearly five decades ago.
summary: Voyager 1 reaches one light‑day distance as historian uncovers Golden Record details.
author: Ars Technica

title: Tesla offers limited $29,900 Cybercab with $299 monthly fee
content: There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla ’s self-driving Cybercab, several. Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s " limited release ” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December. From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road. Read full article Comments
summary: Tesla invited select customers to purchase a two‑seat, gold Cybercab that lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals and is primarily driven by software. The limited release will cost $29,900 with delivery in December and will require a $299 monthly payment to keep it on the road.
author: Ars Technica

title: Waymo halts robotaxi highway driving after DMV cites construction‑zone speed issue
content:
Waymo has limited its robotaxi fleet to surface streets after California’s Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the company to cease highway operations. The DMV’s directive, issued earlier this month, cited the vehicles’ tendency to drive into construction zones at speed and required Waymo to demonstrate that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety” before resuming freeway travel.

The issue follows several incidents in which Waymo robots entered construction zones. In Arizona, the vehicles failed to recognize ramp‑closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April. A month later, seven robotaxis in California entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled nearly 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving, and after the May incidents the company confined its California fleet to surface streets until late July.

In early July, Waymo notified the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it was updating its software. The new version is intended to improve recognition of freeway construction zones, prioritize those zones over other hazards, and reduce speed when a vehicle detects it may be in a construction area.
summary: Waymo is restricting its robotaxi fleet to surface streets after California’s DMV ordered a stop to highway driving because the software entered construction zones at speed. The problem, linked to earlier incidents in Arizona and California, led Waymo to recall almost 3,800 highway‑capable vehicles and begin software updates to better recognize construction zones.
author: Ars Technica

title: ULA says Vulcan rocket failure due to inadequate fuel supply to BE-4 engines
content:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) said on Wednesday that an initial integrated review of flight data from the Vulcan rocket’s launch anomaly on Sunday points to an inadequate fuel supply as the likely source of the problem. The company’s statement noted that the low booster thrust observed during the Leo 1 launch appears to have resulted from insufficient fuel reaching the vehicle’s BE‑4 engines, rather than from any deficiency in the engines themselves.

ULA added that further work is needed to fully determine the cause of the anomaly. The agency’s clarification aligns with a report from Ars Technica published on Tuesday, which indicated that the failure was not attributable to the performance of the Blue Origin‑provided main engines. No additional details about the investigation were provided.
summary: United Launch Alliance said the Vulcan rocket’s launch on Sunday failed because low booster thrust resulted from inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not from engine performance. The company completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly and noted work remains to determine the cause.
author: Ars Technica

title: Specialized Turbo Vado 3 Evo e‑bike reaches 25 mph with 840 Wh battery
content:
Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo e‑bike is reported to deliver high speed and ample power without prompting range‑anxiety for the reviewer. While testing the model, the rider was able to travel through city streets at speeds exceeding 25 mph (40.2 kph) and did not feel the need to monitor battery levels or adjust assist modes to conserve power.

According to the review, the Turbo Vado 3 Evo is equipped with an 840 watt‑hour battery, a peak output of 810 watts and 105 newton‑meters of torque, all supplied by Specialized’s 3.1 motor system. The combination of battery capacity and motor performance allowed the rider to use the highest assist level on hills and maintain high speeds without concern for running out of charge before returning home.
summary: The reviewer tested Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo and rode it at speeds over 25 mph (40.2 kph). The bike’s 840 Wh battery, 810‑watt peak motor and 105 Nm of torque provided ample power without range anxiety.
author: Ars Technica

title: Nvidia clarifies when it will — and won’t — keep financing neoclouds
content: Nvidia clarified its financing policy for “neocloud” projects, stating that the company will only backstop a data‑center loan if the neocloud obtains independent financing and the facility is constructed with Nvidia equipment installed. Interim CEO Colette Kress said Nvidia will not be liable otherwise.
summary: If Nvidia is backstopping a data center loan, it won't be on the hook unless the neocould has independent financing and gets the facility built, with Nvidia gear installed, interim CEO Colette Kress explained.
author: TechCrunch

title: Sam Altman, Greg Brockman Push Back on AI Takeover Debate
content: Sam Altman and Greg Brockman have publicly opposed the growing debate in Silicon Valley about an AI takeover. They acknowledge that advanced models present challenges for maintaining human control. Their remarks emphasize the need for safeguards while addressing concerns over AI dominance.
summary: Sam Altman and Greg Brockman pushed back against Silicon Valley's growing debate over an AI takeover. They acknowledged the challenges of keeping advanced models under human control.
author: TechCrunch

title: David Ellison says HBO will air critical Elon Musk documentary despite $1B investment in Skydance
content: David Ellison said HBO will broadcast a documentary that is highly critical of Elon Musk, even though Musk has made a $1 billion investment in Skydance. The investment has prompted questions about how Musk’s sizable stake might influence Skydance’s plans to distribute the critical film.
summary: Following news of the investment, questions emerged over how Musk's sizable stake in the company might affect Skydance's plans to distribute a documentary that is highly critical of him.
author: TechCrunch

title: Grand Theft Auto VI review highlights fugitive couple Jason and Lucia
content:
A new review of Grand Theft Auto VI describes the game as an unusually realistic and detailed virtual world that blends the series’ trademark chaotic, foul‑mouthed style with a surprising focus on empathy for its central characters. The reviewer likens the breadth of experiences available—ranging from bank robberies and weed‑farm shootouts to gym workouts, shopping, furniture assembly and beach strolls with ice‑cream—to the many possible activities one might encounter in a city like Paris.

The review highlights the fugitive couple at the heart of the story, Jason and Lucia, as the primary lens through which players explore the fictional setting of Leonida. Jason is characterized as muscular, handsome, ex‑military, steady, unflappable, sincere and sparing with words. Lucia is described as a car‑boosting veteran since age 14, possessing a wicked sense of humour, a zero‑tolerance attitude and a propensity for violence that the reviewer found compelling.

At the game’s outset, Lucia is incarcerated while Jason works in the sun‑bathed Keys, employed by a dubious marina figure and living in a run‑down house on stilts with a jetty and a pet snake. After Lucia’s release, the pair attempt to build a new life together, only to become entangled with the wrong people and be forced to flee the modest existence they had begun to create. The reviewer concludes that the game’s multiplicity of activities and its focus on the couple’s story make GTA VI a uniquely expansive and immersive experience.
summary: The review calls Grand Theft Auto VI the most detailed virtual world yet, combining its trademark chaotic crime gameplay with a new emphasis on the fugitive couple Jason and Lucia. It describes Jason as a muscular ex‑military man and Lucia as a lifelong car‑booster, whose story drives the game's many activities.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Wii and PS3 launched in 2006 with opposite visions, each leaving lasting legacy
content:
Both the Nintendo Wii and Sony PlayStation 3 debuted in November 2006, each embodying a markedly different vision for the future of gaming. Nintendo emphasized accessibility, while Sony pursued technical ambition, and both consoles have left a lasting legacy in the industry.

The Wii was presented as an extension of Nintendo’s long‑standing philosophy, described in Japanese as Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō—“lateral thinking with withered technology.” The phrase, created by legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, who also developed the Game Boy, captures the idea of pairing older hardware with innovative concepts to generate new gaming experiences.

Yokoi’s earlier work on the Game Boy illustrated that approach: the handheld used a slow Sharp LR35902 processor and a green monochrome screen, yet it shipped with Tetris, operated on four AA batteries and sold 65 million units—far outpacing contemporary high‑tech rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear.
summary: Both Nintendo and Sony released their consoles in November 2006, with the Wii emphasizing accessibility and the PlayStation 3 emphasizing technical ambition. Each console’s distinct approach has left a lasting legacy in the video‑game industry.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Players take final drive in GTA Online before GTA VI release
content:
For more than a decade, Grand Theft Auto Online’s virtual California has hosted the criminal capers of millions of players. As many prepare to move on to Grand Theft Auto VI, they are marking the end of an era with a collective farewell.

Tonight, the streets of Los Santos will be spared from their usual explosions and high‑speed car chases as hundreds of players gather for a final journey across the game world. The meetup is scheduled before the release of Grand Theft Auto VI at midnight.

Rockstar Games’ multiplayer sandbox typically encourages hostility by providing access to guns, bombs and fighter jets. In this instance, fans chose to peacefully cruise together for “one last drive” in virtual California before the series’ next chapter arrives.
summary: Hundreds of players are cruising peacefully through Los Santos in GTA Online for a final drive before the release of Grand Theft Auto VI at midnight. The gathering marks the end of an era as gamers prepare to move on from the long‑running GTA Online world.
author: Guardian Technology

title: GTA VI live Q&A with games editor Keza MacDonald answers fan questions
content: Grand Theft Auto VI, the biggest games release of the decade, is nearly here. Our games editor Keza MacDonald is online now to answer all your questions Ask a question: log in or sign up here TrickoftheLight asks : Love your review, specifically the part about women finally having something resembling equity and agency instead of being the butt of crass and violent jokes. What did you make of the 30 frames per second rate cap? Did it impede your experience at all?
summary: Grand Theft Auto VI, billed as the decade’s biggest games release, is nearly here. Games editor Keza MacDonald is online for a live session fielding questions about topics such as women’s equity in the game and the 30 fps rate cap.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Pakistani teen’s selfie triggers honour‑killing threat, urging stricter photo moderation
content:
Tech companies have been called on to revise how they moderate online photos, after concerns that certain images can provoke violence against women in some regions. The issue was highlighted by the case of a teenage girl from a conservative Pakistani town who posted a selfie showing her in jeans and a vest‑top—clothing she described as typical for a young woman elsewhere.  

The teenager, identified as Maniza*, said the picture placed her at serious risk of an “honour” killing. She explained that her family is very strict; she always wears a hijab, and her father opposed her attending school until her mother intervened. Maniza recounted that her father warned he would kill her if she got into trouble, a threat she said was serious rather than rhetorical. The incident underscores calls for platforms to consider cultural contexts when moderating visual content.
summary: Tech companies have been urged to adapt moderation of online photos that can trigger violence against women. Maniza, a teenager from a conservative town in Pakistan who never leaves the house without her hijab, says a selfie she took at home could put her at risk of an honour killing.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Best TVs in the UK for every home and screen size, tested
content: Not sure which TV is right for you? Whether you want an affordable mini LED or a feature-packed OLED, here’s what our square-eyed expert recommends • Do you really need to buy a new TV? How to upgrade your setup If your TV looks like an off-cut from Stonehenge, isn’t quite as smart as your microwave or, heaven forfend, is boring old HD rather than 4K HDR (high dynamic range), it could be time to invest in something more up to date. But even a cursory look at the latest TVs available will confirm a bewildering array of options, from super-slim models with unfeasibly large screens to high performers that rival the picture quality at your local cinema.
summary: The guide suggests options ranging from affordable mini LED to feature‑packed OLED models. It explains that viewers with outdated HD sets may want to upgrade to 4K HDR televisions.
author: Guardian Technology

title: US senators ask AI chief Jay Clayton to address infrastructure vulnerabilities after outages
content:
Bipartisan U.S. senators Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds have urged Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and AI czar, to address vulnerabilities in the country’s infrastructure after nationwide outages at major companies and government agencies.

In a letter sent on Tuesday, the senators cited concerns about AI accessing major banks, cyber‑attacks in Japan, and other incidents, calling on Clayton to identify and fix the weaknesses.
summary: US senators ask AI chief Jay Clayton to address infrastructure vulnerabilities after outages.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan plan 30 Mt Middle Corridor capacity by 2029
content: Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan have prepared a joint plan to raise the Middle Corridor’s freight capacity to roughly 30 million tonnes annually by 2029. Concurrently, Belgian firms are in talks about establishing a logistics hub in Kazakhstan and pursuing digital upgrades for the Asia‑Europe trade route.
summary: Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan have drawn up a joint plan to increase Middle Corridor freight capacity to around 30 million tonnes a year by 2029. Belgian companies are discussing a logistics hub in Kazakhstan and digital upgrades to the Asia‑Europe trade route.
author: Euronews

title: Iraqi court sentences six French Islamic State members to life imprisonment
content: An Iraqi court sentenced six French members of Islamic State to life imprisonment. Meanwhile, more than 5,700 Islamic State detainees transferred by the United States from Syria to Iraq are set to begin trial on Sunday, as rights groups question the fairness of Iraq’s courts.
summary: Iraqi court sentenced six French members of the Islamic State to life imprisonment. More than 5,700 Islamic State detainees moved by the United States from Syria to Iraq are set to begin trial on Sunday, while rights groups question whether Iraq’s courts are fair.
author: Euronews

title: Waymo removes driverless taxis from US highways after California ban
content: Waymo has removed its driverless taxis from U.S. highways following a California ban. Regulators labeled the robotaxis an “imminent hazard” after one vehicle attempted to overtake police cars and three others entered an active roadworks zone. The pullback comes as the company readies a European expansion.
summary: Regulators called the robotaxis an "imminent hazard" after one tried to overtake police cars and three others drove into a live roadworks zone. Waymo is pulling the driverless taxis from US highways as it prepares to expand into Europe.
author: Euronews

title: Hakeem Jeffries secures 251 votes, edging toward first Black House speaker
content: New York Democrat Hakeem Jeffries secured 251 votes in favour and 11 against, moving him closer to becoming the first Black speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. He is currently under pressure from progressive lawmakers who are seeking commitments on healthcare, immigration and other key issues.
summary: Hakeem Jeffries secured 251 votes in favour and 11 against. He faces pressure from progressive lawmakers demanding commitments on healthcare, immigration and other key issues.
author: Euronews

title: Houthis advance near Aden, may choose siege over direct assault
content:
Houthi rebels, buoyed by recent victories, moved this week close to Aden, the southern port city that serves as the interim capital of the internationally recognised Yemeni government.  

The possible loss of Aden could permanently shift Yemen’s power balance, given the rebels’ territorial ambitions, regional rivalries, and divisions within government forces.
summary: Houthi rebels, bolstered by recent military successes, advanced close to Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognised Yemeni government, this week. The possible fall of the stronghold could permanently alter the balance of power in Yemen amid territorial ambitions, regional rivalries and divisions within government forces.
author: France 24

title: Palestinians flee Gaza shelters as Israeli army crosses Yellow Line
content: Palestinians fled their tents and shelters in central Gaza on Wednesday after Israel launched a rare ground operation in an area it withdrew ​from under a ‌2025 ceasefire. The Israeli army said it crossed the Yellow Line separating Israeli and Hamas-controlled areas "to remove a threat posed to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip".
summary: Palestinians fled their tents and shelters in central Gaza on Wednesday after Israel launched a rare ground operation in an area it withdrew from under a 2025 ceasefire. The Israeli army said it crossed the Yellow Line separating Israeli and Hamas‑controlled areas to remove a threat to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip.
author: France 24

title: Israel launches new operation targeting Hamas outside Gaza's Yellow Line
content:
Israeli tanks advanced in a central area of the Gaza Strip on Wednesday, witnesses said.

The IDF launched a precise operation within the Gaza Strip earlier today west of the “Yellow Line” to remove a threat posed to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip. The military said its forces were targeting Hamas infrastructure outside the “Yellow Line” that sets the boundary of the part of the enclave controlled by Israel.
summary: Israeli tanks advanced in central Gaza Strip on Wednesday, according to witnesses. The IDF said it was targeting Hamas infrastructure outside the Yellow Line in a precise operation to remove a threat to its troops.
author: France 24

title: Russia's new low‑cost Dan‑T, Filin and Geran‑5 munitions threaten Ukraine
content: Russia has introduced new low‑cost munitions—named Dan‑T, Filin and Geran‑5—that are being widely discussed in Ukraine. According to the report, these weapons are small, fast and inexpensive, and they are specifically designed to bypass Ukrainian anti‑aircraft defenses and reach targets deep inside the country.
summary: Russia has introduced new low‑cost munitions called Dan‑T, Filin and Geran‑5. They are small, fast and cheap weapons designed to evade Ukrainian anti‑aircraft defences and strike deep inside Ukraine.
author: France 24

title: Chuck Schumer faces challenge from Chris Van Hollen as Democrats eye Senate control
content:
Democrats are poised to assume control of the Senate, but incumbent minority leader Chuck Schumer is confronting an insurgent leadership challenge from Senator Chris Van Hollen.  

The dispute over party leadership is revealing divisions within the party about its future direction following the midterms sweep.
summary: As Democrats prepare to take control of the Senate, incumbent minority leader Chuck Schumer is facing an insurgent leadership bid from Senator Chris Van Hollen. Disputes over party leadership are exposing divisions over what direction to take the Democratic party after their midterms sweep.
author: France 24

title: RFI report says French army's secret "Volia" mission hid troops in Ukraine
content: An investigation released by French public radio RFI on November 17 disclosed that the French army’s confidential mission “Volia” has been employed for months to conceal French personnel operating in Ukraine. Following the report, Russia quickly accused France of direct involvement in the conflict.
summary: An investigation published by French public radio channel RFI on November 17 reported that a confidential French army mission called "Volia" has been used for months to conceal French personnel in Ukraine. Russia responded by accusing France of direct involvement in the conflict.
author: France 24

title: Former French PM Édouard Philippe vows spending cuts and raises retirement age to 65
content:
Former prime minister Édouard Philippe announced on Wednesday that he will slash public spending, eliminate France’s statutory 35‑hour workweek and raise the retirement age to 65 from the current 62.9 years. He presented the proposals as a set of measures intended to stave off an economic “catastrophe” for France.

Philippe, once an early frontrunner for next year’s presidential election, is now trailing rivals in opinion polls and faces the possibility of missing the second‑round runoff.
summary: Édouard Philippe announced plans to slash public spending, scrap the statutory 35‑hour workweek and raise the retirement age to 65 from 62.9 years. He is an early presidential frontrunner but is now trailing in opinion polls and risks missing the second‑round runoff.
author: France 24

title: China backs Russia yet sees US as more important, says scholar Kerry Brown
content: Following Xi Jinping's very friendly rare tarmac greeting for Donald Trump, Erin Ogunkeye is pleased to welcome Kerry Brown, Professor of Chinese Studies and Director of the Lau China Institute at King's College, London. Brown examines the complex relationship between the world's two largest economies, China's growing diplomatic influence and the competition over artificial intelligence.“China is the diplomatic center of the world,” says Brown, pointing to Beijing's ability to bring together leaders from Russia, the United States, Europe and elsewhere. He argues that China now has “extraordinary convening power" and significant influence over Russia.
summary: Kerry Brown, professor of Chinese Studies and director of the Lau China Institute at King's College London, said Beijing supports Moscow but views America as more important. He said China is the diplomatic centre of the world with extraordinary convening power and significant influence over Russia.
author: France 24

title: El Salvador's mega-prison becomes model for Latin America amid expert concerns
content: El Salvador’s mega‑prison is being cited by governments throughout Latin America as a template for tackling organized crime. However, experts raise doubts about the model’s effectiveness, its long‑term sustainability and its compatibility with human‑rights standards.
summary: El Salvador's mega-prison has become a model for governments across Latin America seeking to combat organized crime. Experts question whether the approach is effective, sustainable, or compatible with human rights.
author: DW World

title: ICJ to decide if Myanmar's Rakhine operations aimed at Rohingya genocide
content: The International Court of Justice will issue a decision on whether Myanmar’s military operations in Rakhine State about a decade ago were carried out with the intent to destroy the country’s Rohingya minority, in whole or in part. The case concerns allegations of genocide against the Rohingya.
summary: The International Court of Justice is set to decide whether Myanmar's military operations in Rakhine State a decade ago were carried out with intent to destroy the Rohingya minority, in whole or in part. The case addresses allegations of genocide against the Rohingya population.
author: DW World

title: UNICEF urges protection of children as Yemen conflict kills dozens
content: Dozens of children have been killed in Yemen as hostilities intensify. On Wednesday, UNICEF urged the warring parties—Houthi rebels and government forces—to protect children, noting that the renewed fighting is nearing its three‑month anniversary.
summary: Dozens more children have been killed in Yemen as hostilities escalate. UNICEF called on the warring parties, the Houthi rebels and government forces, to protect children as the conflict approaches its three‑month mark.
author: UN News

title: Israel postpones West Bank settlement contracts days after UK sanctions
content:
Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement in the West Bank that analysts say could make a two‑state solution unviable. The delay comes days after the United Kingdom imposed sanctions on building firms operating in the area.

Israeli diplomats said the postponement was not a reaction to the UK sanctions. Attorney General Gali Baharav‑Miara added that any decision on settlement expansion should be taken by a new administration, not by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu.
summary: Israel postpones West Bank settlement contracts days after UK sanctions.
author: Guardian World

title: EU leaders exclude foreign policy chief from Russia peace talks lineup
content:
EU leaders decided to leave the bloc’s foreign‑policy chief out of the negotiating team for upcoming peace talks with Russia. The decision was taken at a summit in Dublin last Friday, where the leaders discussed who should represent the European Union in discussions aimed at ending Russia’s war on Ukraine – described as the gravest security crisis the EU has faced in decades.

The exclusion of the EU’s top diplomat highlights internal disagreements among member states, which the article says undermine the bloc’s ambition to act as a single, clear‑voiced global player in foreign and security matters. The episode illustrates the difficulty the Union faces in presenting a unified stance on the international stage.
summary: EU leaders decided to leave the bloc’s foreign policy chief out of the negotiating team for talks on ending Russia’s war in Ukraine. The decision, made at a summit in Dublin, shows national turf wars are undermining the EU’s goal of speaking with a single voice abroad.
author: Guardian World

title: EnQuest quits North Sea basin; SSE may close Yorkshire gas storage
content:
Labour is confronting a double blow over UK fossil‑fuel projects after two companies signalled a pull‑back of investment. The energy secretary has been dealt a double setback as EnQuest announced it will quit the North Sea oil and gas basin and SSE warned it may close its Yorkshire gas‑storage site, both actions reflecting disagreements with government policy.

EnQuest, described as one of the North Sea’s biggest independent operators, said on Wednesday it is exiting the basin to seek better returns in Asia, citing an “uncertain investment environment within the UK”. SSE’s threat to shut the Yorkshire storage facility adds a second challenge for the government’s energy agenda.
summary: EnQuest announced it is quitting the North Sea oil and gas basin to pursue better returns in Asia, citing an uncertain UK investment environment. SSE has signaled it may close its Yorkshire gas storage site, adding to the energy secretary’s double blow over fossil fuel projects.
author: Guardian World

title: New pro-Brexit campaign surprises Westminster, relies on familiar tactics
content:
A pro‑Brexit campaign was launched this week, a move described as one of the few genuine surprises in Westminster. The campaign’s video, posted on X over the weekend, features footage of riots in France, champagne flowing in Brussels and European politicians claiming desperation for Britain’s cash, employing arguments that the source calls the “most familiar playbook.”  

Meanwhile, No 10 expressed confidence that Burnham can make the case for closer EU ties, citing polling that shows 71 % of voters support that position.
summary: A new pro‑Brexit campaign was launched on X over the weekend, featuring a video that showed riots in France, champagne flowing in Brussels and European politicians saying they were desperate for Britain’s cash. No 10 said it is confident Burnham can make the case for closer EU ties, citing polling that shows 71% voter support.
author: Guardian World

title: Alexander Zverev sued by ex-partner for alleged settlement breach during ATP Finals
content: Men’s world No 1 allegedly violated terms of settlement Lawyers say Zverev will ‘defend himself against lawsuit’ Alexander Zverev was officially notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals on Wednesday. The latest legal case against the men’s world No 1 brought by the mother of the former couple’s daughter alleges that Zverev violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her. The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an interview with the French sports daily L’Equipe earlier this year that “it has been proven that the accusations were false” and “my innocence has been proven”.
summary: Alexander Zverev sued by ex-partner for alleged settlement breach during ATP Finals.
author: Guardian World

title: Researchers claim phantom forests in Australia’s outback used for carbon credits
content:
Researchers from the Australian National University and the University of New South Wales say they examined 50 forest‑regeneration projects in Australia’s semi‑arid outback and found that the projects have produced only a small increase in forest and canopy cover, even after wet conditions. The researchers describe the resulting “phantom forests” as being used to generate carbon credits that offset emissions from fossil‑fuel companies.

Carbon‑credit companies have rejected the research findings, disputing the claim that the regeneration areas have contributed minimal forest growth. The disagreement has revived debate over the legitimacy of Australia’s climate‑change policy and the role of carbon offsets in the country.
summary: Researchers said phantom forests in the semi‑arid outback are being used to create carbon credits that offset emissions. Carbon‑credit companies rejected the research, which examined 50 forest regeneration projects and found only a small increase in forest and canopy cover despite wet conditions.
author: Guardian World

title: Analysis finds Business Council of Australia aligns with fossil fuel industry over members' values
content:
Research by InfluenceMap finds that the Business Council of Australia (BCA) is lobbying for policies that expand gas supplies, a stance the analysis says conflicts with the climate concerns expressed by most of the council’s members. The study highlights the influence of a small number of major companies on the association’s positions.

The research also notes that the BCA does not publicly identify the members of its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns about how its policies are formed and whose interests they reflect.
summary: Research by InfluenceMap says the Business Council of Australia is lobbying for gas expansion policies that conflict with the climate concerns of most of its members. The association also does not publicly disclose the members of its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns about how its policies are shaped.
author: Guardian World

title: Fears grow that US will impose sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling
content:
Fears are growing that the United States could impose sanctions on judges at the International Court of Justice, including Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.  

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for genocide, and previous cases have hinged on proving “intent” to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. A ruling against Myanmar could also set a precedent for the court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza.
summary: Fears grow that US will impose sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling.
author: Guardian World

title: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries as US House speaker
content: Democrats have nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as Speaker of the United States House of Representatives. The nomination places him on a trajectory to become the first Black lawmaker to lead the chamber, should Democrats assume control of the House in January.
summary: Democrats have nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker of the US House of Representatives. The nomination puts him on a path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber when Democrats take control in January.

title: William and Kate meet Modi in New Delhi, reflect on enduring UK‑India ties
content: The meeting in New Delhi was a late addition to the royal couple's India visit, which has also included their appearance at the annual Earthshot Prize
summary: William and Kate met Modi in New Delhi and said the relationship between the UK and India is enduring. The meeting was a late addition to their India visit, which also included an appearance at the annual Earthshot Prize.

title: Swing when you’re winning? Biggest leaps across Fifa’s football rankings | The Knowledge
content:
Bogdan Kotarlic inquired whether the 75-place difference between Scotland’s highest Fifa ranking of 13th in 2007 and its lowest of 88th in 2005 represented the largest gap for a national team. Pete Tomlin calculated that this swing places Scotland joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles, meaning it is not the largest disparity in men’s international football.

Other home nations have experienced more dramatic fluctuations. Wales moved up 109 places from 117th to eighth under managers Gary Speed and Chris Coleman, while Northern Ireland rose from 129th in 2004 to 20th in 2017, also a 109-place improvement.

The article lists several nations with larger ranking swings, led by Montenegro with a 183-place difference between its best (16th) and worst (199th) positions. Other teams with significant gaps include Kuwait (165 places), Bosnia and Herzegovina (160 places), and Cape Verde (155 places). The list continues with Central African Republic, Libya, Equatorial Guinea, Moldova, El Salvador, Cuba, and Slovakia, which all recorded swings ranging from 136 to 153 places.
summary: Swing when you’re winning? Biggest leaps across Fifa’s football rankings | The Knowledge.
author: Guardian Sport

title: 14-year-old Leihani Zoric wins ISA Open World Surfing title in Peru
content: Zoric puts target on veteran teammate Gilmore’s back: ‘I want to be like her’ Peru win makes her first Indigenous Australian world champion in open category With the surfing world her oyster, Leihani Zoric has set her sights stratospherically high after the 14-year-old stunned a star-studded field to be crowned the youngest ever ISA Open World Surfing Champion and claim a second world title this year. Zoric, who was still 13 when she won the ISA under-18 world title in September, added a gold medal to her burgeoning individual palmarès with victory in Peru over the weekend, when she emerged triumphant ahead of established stars of the surfing world such as Stephanie Gilmore, Tyler Wright, Carissa Moore and Johanne Defay.
summary: Leihani Zoric became the youngest ever ISA Open World Surfing Champion by defeating Stephanie Gilmore and other stars in Peru. The 14-year-old, who is the first Indigenous Australian world champion in the open category, now holds two world titles this year.
author: Guardian Sport

title: ‘Time for a circuit breaker’: Cricket Australia creates forum for players to air views on sandpapergate
content:
Cricket Australia has established an independent forum for players and staff to share their accounts of the 2018 South Africa tour, aiming to act as a “circuit breaker” for the ongoing sandpaper controversy. Interim CA chair David Boon and chief executive Todd Greenberg stated that the initiative is not intended to “re-litigate” events from eight years ago. They emphasized that no further sanctions are expected regardless of the forum’s findings.

The announcement was made by Boon and Greenberg near a children’s playground outside Bellerive Oval in Hobart, prior to the third one-day international between Australia and England. The move follows questions from player Usman Khawaja, who asked, “Are we just going in a circle here?” regarding the prolonged nature of the issue.
summary: ‘Time for a circuit breaker’: Cricket Australia creates forum for players to air views on sandpapergate.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Australia v England – third and deciding men’s one-day cricket international – live
content:
The third and deciding men’s one-day international between Australia and England is currently underway at Bellerive Oval in Hobart, with the hosts chasing a target of 329 runs to secure victory. While the match proceeds, attention has also turned to statements regarding the Australian cricket team’s culture and recent controversies.

Australian Cricket (CA) CEO Todd Greenberg addressed the ongoing situation, noting that for the past week, there have been several conflicting accounts of events that occurred in Cape Town in 2018. Greenberg described the period as incredibly difficult and uncomfortable for the game and those involved. He acknowledged that CA played a part in creating the culture that existed at the time, which is linked to what happened then and continues to play out now.

In response to the controversy, CA has established an independent forum to allow all parties who wish to participate to share their versions of events. Greenberg emphasized that this process is not an investigation and does not aim to produce sanctions. Participation is entirely voluntary, and no one is forced to take part. He stated that the forum provides a safe setting for individuals to have a voice, noting that the events in question took place eight and a half years ago.

The CA leadership expressed pride in the culture the team has built over the past eight years, giving credit to the players, leaders, and coaches. Specific mention was made of Pat and Andrew, who continue to lead the team with distinction. However, the organization also recognized the pain and hurt caused by the events surrounding sandpaper. Greenberg urged respect for the process and hoped that players would be afforded the space to perform at their best during this important period for the game.
summary: Australia v England – third and deciding men’s one-day cricket international – live.

title: F1's Three US Grands Prix: Austin, Miami, Las Vegas Compared
content: Formula 1, which previously struggled to establish itself in the United States, now hosts three grands prix. A comparison examines the merits of the Austin, Miami, and Las Vegas events, highlighting their distinct characteristics such as cowboy boots, cocktails, and casinos.
summary: F1 has struggled to establish itself in the United States but now hosts three grands prix. The article compares the merits of Austin, Miami and Las Vegas.

Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) criticized acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao’s analogy regarding food shortages on Navy vessels, suggesting the comparison undermined reports of poor conditions aboard ships docked in the Middle East. title: Stephen A. Smith defends not challenging Trump’s claims on Black Americans
content:
ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith defended his choice not to push back on President Trump’s claims about his record with Black Americans during a recent interview, arguing that viewers deserved to hear the president’s full thoughts without constant interruptions.  

The remarks came during last week’s episode of Smith’s “Straight Shooter” podcast, where Trump had called Smith.

content: Video circulating on social media depicts ICE officers throwing Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, a 23-year-old pregnant U.S. citizen, to the ground. The incident occurred during her detainment outside a jail.

content: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, a spokesperson for Chair Tim Scott (R‑S. C.) confirmed Tuesday. title: Delhi devotees brave polluted Yamuna for Chhath festival
content:
In Delhi, Hindu devotees gathered at the Yamuna River for the Chhath festival, wading through patches of toxic foam created by a mixture of pollutants that included industrial chemicals and untreated sewage.

The Chhath festival is observed by Indian and Nepalese Hindus to honor Lord Surya, the sun god, and the goddess Chhathi Maiya. The celebrations are intended to bring a prosperous life, fertility, and protection.
summary: In Delhi, Hindu devotees gathered at the Yamuna River for the Chhath festival, wading through toxic foam from industrial chemicals and untreated sewage. The festival honors Lord Surya and goddess Chhathi Maiya, celebrating prosperity, fertility, and protection.
